story: Cangjie was an official historian serving the Yellow Emperor and is credited as the inventor of Chinese characters. According to legend he had four eyes, and when he completed his invention of the characters, deities and ghosts wept and the sky rained millet. One version of his legend tells that shortly after unifying China, the Yellow Emperor grew dissatisfied with the old method of recording information by tying knots in rope, and charged Cangjie with creating a system of written characters. Cangjie settled on a riverbank and devoted himself to the task, but for a long time could not create even one character. One day he saw a phoenix flying overhead carrying an object in its beak; the object fell before him and proved to be a hoof-print. Unable to identify the animal, he asked a passing hunter, who told him it was the unmistakable hoof-print of a Pixiu, distinct from that of any other beast. This exchange inspired Cangjie to believe that capturing the distinguishing characteristics of things in drawings would produce the ideal form of writing. He began studying the sun, moon, stars, clouds, lakes, rivers, oceans, and every kind of bird and beast, creating characters based on their special traits, until he had compiled a great many. He presented the completed writing system to the Yellow Emperor, who summoned the premiers of the nine provinces so that Cangjie could teach them the new characters. Monuments and temples were later built in his honor on the riverbank where he had worked. Another version of the legend says Cangjie was instead inspired by observing the network of veins on a turtle.
